newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-JOHANSSON HINTS HE STILL BACKS GERMANY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-JOHANSSON HINTS HE STILL BACKS GERMANY.

text.p: UEFA chief Lennart Johansson hinted on Tuesday he would still be backing Germany for the 2006 World Cup finals despite the fact the European governing body has put off a final decision about its top candidate.
Johansson and UEFA's executive committee originally supported Germany's bid completely before going back on their decision last week following outrage in England which also wants the finals.

But the UEFA president said: "The members of the executive committee know what they wanted. I can't say whether anybody is going to change their mind. I have to remain objective. But that doesn't mean I'm changing my mind.
"I know what decision I made and I know who was there," he said in an interview with the German news agency SID in Cyprus.

Germany launched their bid in 1993 and got the full backing of UEFA which is keen to avoid the kind of battle in Europe which South Korea and Japan fought in Asia for the 2002 tournament. The event was eventually awarded to both countries.
But after a meeting in London last Friday, UEFA withdrew its total support for Germany and agreed to meet officials from both England and Germany in April to decide which bid to back.

"I must admit that there has been a lack of communication since England first showed interest in the tournament...Both countries are capable of holding the World Cup," Johansson said in the interview.
"We have to do everything to avoid a confrontation between England and Germany. We're not very happy with the situation."
On Monday the respected German football magazine Kicker accused UEFA of kow-towing to British political pressure by withdrawing its unequivocal support of the German bid.
UEFA general secretary Gerhard Aigner told Germany's Sueddeutsche Zeitung on Tuesday that he believed politics was playing a role in Britain.
"Politics is heavily involved in England. That is why we were gruff because they had never put their opinion to us officially before," he said.
"In this way the German soccer federation (DFB), which since 1993 has never shown its interest by running a campaign, has now been overtaken on the inside."
